newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu adviser favours Israel budget cut.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu adviser favours Israel budget cut.

text.p: The chief economic adviser to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Monday he favours a budget cut if there is a deviation from the deficit target but it must be tied to an interest rate reduction.

"It is clear that the injection that the economy needs is an expansion, even minimal, of monetary policy. As far as fiscal policy is concerned we are with our fingers on the trigger and if another budget cut is required it should be undertaken," Moshe Leon told reporters at a briefing in Jerusalem.

Netanyahu, Finance Minister Dan Meridor and Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel met on Sunday evening to discuss the budget deficit but no decision was reached and the talks will resume on Monday afternoon.
The 1997 budget of 197 billion shekels already includes a seven billion shekel cut. But Treasury officials believe another one billion shekel cut may be needed to meet the deficit target.
Leon said that in the first quarter of this year there was a 500 million shekel deviation from the deficit target.

"It seems to me there is a need for another (budget) cut but in any event any cut must be accompanied by a more expansionary monetary policy," Leon said. He added that all the economic indicators show it is possible to lower interest rates.
Israel's economy is slowing and a source at the meeting quoted Meridor as saying gross domestic product would grow only three percent in 1997, less than the forecast four percent.
While the Bank of Israel has urged cutting the budget, it refuses to link such a move with a reduction in interest rates.
Leon expressed disappointment in the Treasury's decision to freeze plans for tax reform.
"There is no doubt that some sort of tax reform has to be done, even a long-term progrmame," Leon said.
The Treasury has said it cannot lower taxes when government revenues are lagging its target.

Leon said privatisation was proceeding according to plan. He announced that the parliamentary finance committe on Monday approved the government's plan to sell an additional 25 percent of Bezeq Israel Telecom this year.
He said the government intends to sell off its remaining shares in Israel Chemicals CHIM.TA but it is not certain this will be done this year.
Leon said a committee formed to study the privatisation of El Al Israel Airlines will present its recommendations in May.
Leon, who heads the committee, would not disclose details but said: "In principle we always prefer having the public participate in privatisations and selling shares on the stock exchange."
In 1998 and 1999 the government would like to privatise the Industrial Development Bank, oil Refineries and possibly defence companies, he said.
